beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude UI, ask shown answered; IN-FOR-BEAR LAW (Liam, in for Ameya)
beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Ameya. Build it with Claude, then take it apart. Margin lets you trade with borrowed money. It can double your gains — and it is the fastest way I know to lose more than you ever put in. Here is the machinery.

props.command: claude "explain margin and short selling — show how leverage cuts both ways, with a real margin-call example"
output: 2:1 leverage — $10k of cash controls $20k of stock
a 20% drop in the stock = a 40% hit to your equity
short selling: the loss has no ceiling

beats.role_note: concept illustration (Manim) — leverage as buying power; ILLUSTRATE LAW
beats.narration_text: Start with ten thousand dollars in cash. Under Regulation T, your broker lets you borrow an equal amount — fifty percent initial margin — so you control twenty thousand dollars of stock. That is two-to-one leverage. If the stock rises ten percent, you don't make a thousand dollars, you make two — a twenty percent gain on your cash. On the way up, leverage looks like free money.
beats.visual_intent: cash $10k box + broker loan $10k box = $20k buying power; 2:1 leverage; +10% stock -> +$2,000 (+20% on cash)

beats.role_note: concept illustration (Manim) — the loan is fixed, so equity takes the amplified hit
beats.narration_text: Now run it the other way. The stock falls twenty percent. Your twenty-thousand-dollar position is worth sixteen — but you still owe the ten-thousand-dollar loan. The debt does not shrink. Your equity just went from ten thousand to six thousand. A twenty percent drop in the stock is a forty percent hit to you. Leverage doesn't pick a direction; it multiplies whichever one you get.
beats.visual_intent: stacked bars before/after: position $20k->$16k, loan fixed $10k (grey), equity $10k->$6k (terracotta->red); punch line: stock -20% -> equity -40%

beats.role_note: concept illustration (Manim) — the margin call mechanism
beats.narration_text: And it gets worse, because you don't control the exit. Your broker sets a maintenance margin — say thirty percent. The moment your equity divided by market value slips under that line, they issue a margin call and can sell your stock out from under you. With a ten-thousand-dollar loan, that trigger is a portfolio value of fourteen thousand, two hundred eighty-six dollars. You get forced out near the bottom — exactly when you'd want to hold.
beats.visual_intent: falling portfolio-value curve; margin readout 50% -> 37.5%; dashed maintenance line at 30%; MARGIN CALL fires; forced sale at $14,286

beats.role_note: concept illustration (Manim) — the loss asymmetry; short squeeze
beats.narration_text: Short selling is the mirror image: you borrow the stock, sell it, and profit if it falls. But look at the asymmetry. Buy a stock, and the worst case is it goes to zero — you lose one hundred percent, and no more. Short a stock, and there is no ceiling. It can double, triple, ten-x, and your loss climbs right past one hundred percent with no limit. That is the short squeeze — a rising price forcing shorts to buy back, driving it higher still.
beats.visual_intent: two loss columns: LONG capped at -100% (grey, 'can only go to zero'); SHORT unbounded (red) with an up-arrow, '-100% -> -200% -> no limit'; short-squeeze line

beats.narration_text: So here is the honest verdict. Margin is a multiplier, not a strategy. It amplifies your gains, it amplifies your losses, and it hands your broker the power to force the exit. Used with your eyes open, it is a tool. Used as a shortcut to bigger returns, it is how accounts go to zero.
beats.visual_intent: recap checklist: amplifies gains / amplifies losses / hands broker your exit; big line 'A multiplier, not a strategy.'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in, read & discussed; greeting 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt into Claude with your own numbers — your cash, your stock, your broker's maintenance margin — and have it compute your leverage ratio and your exact margin-call price. Then ask the question that actually matters: how far can this position fall before someone else decides to sell it? Know that number before you borrow a single dollar.

props.command: claude "I have $8,000 cash and want to buy AAPL at $220 on 50% margin, 30% maintenance margin. Compute my leverage ratio, my margin-call price, and how far the stock can fall before a margin call."

beats.narration_text: Leverage cuts both ways. Know the downside before you borrow. This is Liam, in for Ameya.
